messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Fast Food Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 64

He is 41, a Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his adult life working in fast food kitchens, the kind of work that rewards speed, routine, and the ability to keep moving no matter what is happening around you. He says he used to like that about it. Before everything changed, he took pride in being dependable. He opened the restaurant some mornings, closed it on others, knew how long the oil needed to heat, how to calm an impatient customer, how to smile even when his feet hurt. He lived alone, kept to himself, sent money when he could to family overseas, and told himself that a quiet life was a good life.

The event he returns to again and again happened three years ago, at the bus stop after a late shift. He had finished cleaning the grill and taking out trash, and he remembers being tired in the ordinary way, already thinking about sleep. A young man and woman were arguing near the curb. At first he tried not to pay attention. He says where he grew up, and even here, you learn not to stare at other people’s trouble. Then the argument changed. The man shoved the woman hard enough that she hit the bench. There was shouting, the sound of tires, someone dropping a bag. He remembers freezing. He says this part with shame, though his body seems still caught in that moment. He saw the man pull out a knife. He saw the woman put her hands up. He heard her scream once, then again, shorter the second time. Other people started yelling. Someone ran. He could not move until after the attacker fled. By then there was blood on the sidewalk and on the woman’s coat, too much of it, and he was kneeling beside her with his hands shaking so badly he could barely hold his phone.

He gave a statement to police that night and another one later, but what stays with him is not the paperwork. It is the bright white of the bus stop light on the pavement, the smell of exhaust mixed with blood, and the way her eyes seemed to look past him. In the weeks afterward, he told himself he should be grateful he was not the one attacked. Instead he began sleeping in fragments. As soon as he closed his eyes, he saw the knife coming up again. Sometimes in the dream he is the one being stabbed; sometimes he is standing in place while everyone else moves around him, and he wakes with his heart racing and his shirt damp. He starts leaving the television on all night because silence makes the images louder.

At work, the fryer hissing begins to sound like the rush of cars from that night. When customers raise their voices, even over something small like a wrong order, his shoulders jump before he can stop himself. A coworker once drops a metal tray behind him and he spins around so fast he knocks over a stack of cups. After that, he notices people watching him. He feels embarrassed, then angry at himself for being embarrassed. He starts volunteering for prep in the back so he does not have to stand near the front windows facing the street.

His world gets smaller in practical ways first. He changes bus routes to avoid that stop, even though the new route takes longer and makes him late sometimes. He turns down evening shifts when he can. He stops walking anywhere after dark. He no longer sits with coworkers after work, even the ones he likes. When his manager asks why he always seems tense, he shrugs and says he is not sleeping well. It is easier than explaining that every stranger who argues on the sidewalk pulls his body back into that moment before the knife appears.

He also carries a heavy, repetitive guilt. He wonders if he should have shouted sooner, stepped in sooner, done something that might have changed the outcome. Intellectually he knows there was a weapon and that other people froze too, but his mind returns to the same accusation: You stood there. This thought comes especially when he is alone in his apartment after work, shoes still on, replaying the scene instead of eating dinner. He has become thinner over the past year. He says food is around him all day, but often he has no appetite by the time he gets home.

People around him know him now as quiet, but he says he was not always this guarded. He used to call his siblings often. Now he avoids their calls when he feels on edge because he does not want them to hear it in his voice. He startles at sirens, scans exits when he enters any room, and sits where he can see the door. On crowded buses he watches everyone’s hands. If a couple begins arguing, his chest tightens and his mouth goes dry. He tells himself to breathe, to look away, to remember he is here and not there, but his body does not believe him. Even on calmer days he feels as if danger is only briefly hidden, never really gone.
